target_customer: Health-conscious consumers paying a monthly subscription for personalized liquid vitamins
problem: Generic pill supplements ignore body composition and genetics; Nutrigene made liquid supplements formulated from a quiz, optional 23andMe DNA data and blood tests.
business_model: Monthly subscription of personalized liquid supplements, packages from about 99 dollars per month

founders.name: Min FitzGerald
prior_employers: Singularity (launched the startup out of it)
founders.background_notes: Launch HN post: over 10 years as a personal trainer, health coach and behavioral scientist in food and consumer goods. TechCrunch 2018-02-05.

founders.name: Van Duesterberg
education: PhD in biophysics and epigenetics, Stanford
founders.background_notes: Biotech and epigenetics background per TechCrunch 2018-02-05 and the Launch HN post, which says over 10 years of research on environmental effects on gene expression. Not listed on the YC page, which names only Min FitzGerald.

exit.reason: Not public; directories list the company as closed or inactive

competitors.name: Off-the-shelf supplements from Amazon and Walgreens
competitors.what: Generic vitamins and supplements sold at retail, the incumbents named by the founders

technical_complexity.rationale: A quiz and DNA upload driving a formulation lookup plus small batch liquid compounding is modest engineering; the hard part was scientific and regulatory backing, which commenters questioned.

defensibility.rationale: Formulation logic was proprietary only in claim, with no published efficacy research, and other personalized supplement firms could copy the model.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent action found; the company is recorded as closed.

market_need_then: Personalized nutrition was a rising trend in 2017 and 2018, and TechCrunch reported 8,500 personalized dosages shipped by September 2018, but Hacker News commenters doubted the efficacy evidence.

branding.domain_note: Used mynutrigene.com with a my prefix; a separate Nutrigene LLC held a NUTRIGENE trademark (now dead) and other companies share the name.

identity.voice_and_tone: Marketing claims were challenged as overreaching in the Launch HN thread

branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch in February and September 2018; the Launch HN thread was skeptical.

brand_strength.rationale: Two TechCrunch pieces gave some visibility, but no brand assets or community were found and the name is shared with other firms.

outcome_analysis: Nutrigene sold personalized liquid supplements, joined YC in Winter 2018 and raised about 120 thousand dollars, per a database. TechCrunch reported 8,500 dosages shipped by September 2018 at roughly 99 dollars a month. Directories later list it as closed, but no shutdown notice or post-mortem was found, so the cause is not public. Launch HN commenters questioned the efficacy evidence and privacy, which are possible risks but not stated causes.
notes: The YC page lists no website; mynutrigene.com is named in a TechCrunch listing and a fetch returned no content, so the site is treated as dead or unverified. The 120K round rests on CB Insights (labeled seed) and Bouncewatch (pre-seed dated 2018-03-22); stage chosen pre_seed with the label conflict noted; TechCrunch Battlefield page also shows 120,000 raised and closed status. Founding year conflicts (2016 vs 2017). The founders' school for FitzGerald was not found. The cause of closure is not public, so failure_factors stays empty. The retail competitors are those the founders name in the launch thread, not funded startups; personalized nutrition firms like Habit and Viome were not verified with a dated source.
